profiles.name: UK mains voltage (current law)
profiles.about: The statutory supply in Great Britain: 230 V +10% / -6%, so 216.2 V to 253 V (the ESQCR 2002). Many homes sit at 240-250 V, which is normal. Solar inverters trip at about 262 V. See also the ENA's 2026 proposal, which would lower the minimum to 207 V.

bands.message: Mains far too low: under 207 V
Mains below the legal minimum (216.2 V)
Mains above the legal maximum (253 V)
Mains far too high: solar inverters trip about here

profiles.name: UK mains voltage (ENA proposed, 2026)
profiles.about: The Energy Networks Association's 2026 proposal: 230 V +/-10%, so 207 V to 253 V, giving networks room for rooftop solar and EV chargers without tripping equipment at the top. Not law yet (it goes to DESNZ); use it once it is. Below 195.5 V (-15%) is critical.

bands.message: Mains far too low: under 195.5 V
Mains below the legal minimum (207 V)
Mains above the legal maximum (253 V)
Mains far too high: solar inverters trip about here

profiles.name: UK grid frequency
profiles.about: The statutory frequency is 50 Hz +/-1%, so 49.5-50.5 Hz; the grid normally holds 49.8-50.2 Hz, and automatic load shedding starts at about 48.8 Hz. The same everywhere on the grid: watch it on one meter.

bands.message: Frequency below the legal minimum (49.5 Hz)
Frequency above the legal maximum (50.5 Hz)

profiles.name: US mains voltage (120 V, ANSI C84.1)
profiles.about: ANSI C84.1 for 120 V service: Range A (114-126 V) is where supply should be; Range B (110-127 V) is acceptable now and then, and the utility should correct it. Each leg of a 120/240 V split-phase supply is 120 V.

bands.message: Mains far too low: under 104 V
Mains below ANSI Range B (110 V)
Mains below ANSI Range A (114 V)
Mains above ANSI Range A (126 V)
Mains above ANSI Range B (127 V)
Mains far too high: over 132 V

profiles.name: US grid frequency (60 Hz)
profiles.about: North American grids run at 60 Hz, held very close to it; automatic under-frequency load shedding starts at 59.3 Hz (NERC), and 59.3-60.7 Hz is the steady-state range. The same everywhere on an interconnection: watch it on one meter.

bands.message: Grid emergency: load shedding starts (59.3 Hz)

profiles.name: EU mains voltage (230 V, EN 50160)
profiles.about: EN 50160, the European supply standard: 230 V +/-10% (207-253 V) for 95% of each week, and never below -15% (195.5 V). Countries may set their own limits too (the UK's is +10% / -6%; see its own profiles).

bands.message: Mains far too low: under 195.5 V
Mains far too high: over 264.5 V

profiles.name: EU grid frequency (50 Hz)
profiles.about: EN 50160: 49.5-50.5 Hz for 99.5% of the year. The continental grid normally holds 49.8-50.2 Hz; load shedding starts at about 49.0 Hz (ENTSO-E's plan, from memory: check before relying on it). Watch it on one meter.

profiles.name: Japan mains voltage (100 V)
profiles.about: Japan's 100 V supply must be kept at 101 V +/-6 V (95-107 V), under the Electricity Business Act's rules (from memory: the search didn't turn up the text). For the frequency: eastern Japan is 50 Hz (use the EU profile), western Japan 60 Hz (use the US one).

bands.message: Mains far too low: under 90 V
Mains below the legal minimum (95 V)
Mains above the legal maximum (107 V)
Mains far too high: over 110 V

profiles.name: China mains voltage (220 V, GB/T 12325)
profiles.about: GB/T 12325: a 220 V single-phase supply may deviate -10% to +7% (198-235.4 V).

bands.message: Mains far too low: under 187 V
Mains below the standard's minimum (198 V)
Mains above the standard's maximum (235.4 V)
Mains far too high: over 242 V

profiles.name: China grid frequency (50 Hz, GB/T 15945)
profiles.about: GB/T 15945: the frequency may deviate +/-0.2 Hz in normal running (+/-0.5 Hz on small systems; from memory: the search didn't turn up the text). Watch it on one meter.

profiles.name: Australia mains voltage (230 V, AS 60038)
profiles.about: AS 60038: 230 V +10% / -6% (216.2-253 V), the same limits as Great Britain. Rooftop solar pushes many streets towards the top.

bands.message: Mains far too low: under 207 V
Mains below the standard's minimum (216.2 V)
Mains above the standard's maximum (253 V)
Mains far too high: solar inverters trip about here

profiles.name: Australia grid frequency (50 Hz)
profiles.about: The NEM's frequency operating standard keeps 49.85-50.15 Hz in normal running (from memory: check the AEMC's standard); outside 49.5-50.5 Hz is a serious event. Watch it on one meter.

profiles.name: UK inverter trips: voltage (G98/G99)
profiles.about: How close the supply is to tripping a grid-tied inverter (a Sunsynk or any other) under G98/G99: under 200.1 V for 2.5 s or over 262.2 V for 1 s trips it; under 184 V or over 273.7 V trips it in 0.5 s. Installers can set these per network operator, so check your inverter's own grid settings match.

bands.message: Under G99 stage 2 (184 V): inverters trip in 0.5 s
Under G99 stage 1 (200.1 V): inverters trip after 2.5 s
Mains below the legal minimum (216.2 V)
Mains above 253 V: close to the inverter's trip (262.2 V)
Over G99 stage 1 (262.2 V): inverters trip after 1 s
Over G99 stage 2 (273.7 V): inverters trip in 0.5 s

profiles.name: UK inverter trips: frequency (G98/G99)
profiles.about: How close the grid's frequency is to tripping a grid-tied inverter under G98/G99: under 47.5 Hz for 20 s or over 51.5 Hz for 90 s trips it; under 47 Hz or over 52 Hz in 0.5 s. Check your inverter's own grid settings match.

bands.message: Under G99 stage 2 (47 Hz): inverters trip in 0.5 s
Under G99 stage 1 (47.5 Hz): inverters trip after 20 s
Over G99 stage 1 (51.5 Hz): inverters trip after 90 s
Over G99 stage 2 (52 Hz): inverters trip in 0.5 s

profiles.name: Leak (on/off)
profiles.about: A leak sensor: dry is all well; wet is critical, at once.

profiles.name: Smoke (on/off)
profiles.about: A smoke alarm: critical the moment it trips.

profiles.name: Gas (on/off)
profiles.about: A gas detector: critical the moment it trips.

profiles.name: Carbon monoxide (on/off)
profiles.about: A carbon monoxide alarm: critical the moment it trips.

profiles.name: Safety (on/off)
profiles.about: Anything Home Assistant calls a safety sensor: on means unsafe, critical at once.

profiles.name: Tamper (on/off)
profiles.about: A tamper switch (a sensor's case opened): a warning.

profiles.name: Problem (on/off)
profiles.about: A device reporting a problem: an error.

profiles.name: Door (on/off)
profiles.about: A door contact: closed is all well; open is a task (for a door that should be shut, make it a warning).

profiles.name: Garage door (on/off)
profiles.about: A garage door contact: open is a task.

profiles.name: Window (on/off)
profiles.about: A window contact: open is a task.

profiles.name: Opening (on/off)
profiles.about: Any opening contact: open is a task.

profiles.name: Window or cover: closed (states)
profiles.about: A cover (a roof window, blind, shutter or garage door): closed is all well; open, or anything else, is a task. For a skylight that must shut when it rains, Duplicate… it and make open a warning.

profiles.name: Connected (on/off)
profiles.about: A device's connection: disconnected is an error.

profiles.name: Update available (on/off)
profiles.about: An update entity: one waiting is a task.

profiles.name: Lock: locked (states)
profiles.about: A lock: locked is all well; unlocked is a task; jammed is an error.

profiles.name: Alarm panel (states)
profiles.about: An alarm panel: disarmed, armed, arming and pending are all well; triggered is critical, at once; anything else a warning.

profiles.name: Robot vacuum (states)
profiles.about: A robot vacuum: docked, cleaning, returning, idle or paused are all well; anything else (error, stuck) is an error.

profiles.name: Robot mower (states)
profiles.about: A robot mower: docked, mowing, returning or paused are all well; anything else is an error.

profiles.name: Battery, replaceable (%)
profiles.about: A replaceable battery's level (a sensor's coin cell or AAs): replace it below 20%, flat below 5%. The same as Sensor Watch's default for battery sensors; unavailable is often the battery that died.

profiles.name: Rechargeable battery, 20-80% (%)
profiles.about: State of charge for lithium (NMC) packs kept to 20-80% for a long life: most EVs' daily limit, laptops, power tools. Above 80% is fine before a long trip, but left there it wears the cells; below 20% wants charging.

bands.message: Above 80%: fine for a trip, don't leave it there

profiles.name: Rechargeable battery, 20-85% (%)
profiles.about: State of charge for lithium packs with a little more headroom than 80%. Above 85% is fine before a long trip, but left there it wears the cells; below 20% wants charging.

bands.message: Above 85%: fine for a trip, don't leave it there

profiles.name: Rechargeable battery, 20-90% (%)
profiles.about: State of charge for lithium packs charged to 90% day to day. Above 90% is fine before a long trip, but left there it wears the cells; below 20% wants charging.

bands.message: Above 90%: fine for a trip, don't leave it there

profiles.name: Rechargeable battery, 20-100% (LiFePO4) (%)
profiles.about: State of charge for LiFePO4 (LFP) packs, which are happy full (and want a full charge now and then to balance): most home and inverter batteries, LFP EVs.

profiles.name: Home battery at its reserve (%)
profiles.about: An inverter's battery (a Sunsynk's, say) runs down every night by design, so low isn't a fault: this only says when it reaches a 10% reserve and the house leans on the grid.

bands.message: Home battery at its reserve: the house is on grid power

profiles.name: Lead-acid 12 V battery (V)
profiles.about: A 12 V lead-acid battery's voltage (a car's, a leisure battery, a UPS): at rest 12.6 V is full, 12.4 V about 75%, 12.2 V half, 11.8 V flat; 13.8-14.7 V while charging. Read at rest for the charge; left flat, it sulphates.

bands.message: Flat: charge it now, before it sulphates
Far over-charged: check the charger now

profiles.name: LiFePO4 12 V battery (V)
profiles.about: A 12 V LiFePO4 battery (four cells): about 13.2-13.4 V at rest when charged, 14.2-14.6 V charging; its voltage is flat until nearly empty, so the low bands are rough.

bands.message: Far over-charged: check the charger now

profiles.name: LiFePO4 cell (V)
profiles.about: One LiFePO4 cell, as a battery's BMS reports it: 3.0-3.45 V in use; under 2.5 V or over 3.65 V harms it.

bands.message: Cell at the top of its charge

profiles.name: Low battery (on/off)
profiles.about: A device's low-battery warning (on/off rather than a percentage): replace it.

profiles.name: Broadband download: ADSL (16 Mbps)
profiles.about: A speed test's download (Mbps) against a 16 Mbps plan: 70% or more is fine; below half, worth taking up with the provider. The hold-off is just over an hour, so with hourly tests it takes two poor ones in a row.

bands.message: Barely working: under 10% of the plan
Well below the plan: under half

profiles.name: Pool or hot tub pH
profiles.about: Ideal 7.4-7.6; 7.2-7.8 is acceptable (the CDC says the same for pools and hot tubs: pH is the same chemistry in both). Below, the water is acidic and corrosive; above, chlorine stops working and scale forms. Works for a probe or an input_number you type test-strip readings into.

bands.message: pH far too low: corrosive, etches surfaces
pH far too high: chlorine mostly inactive, scale forms

profiles.name: Pool or hot tub pH (detailed)
profiles.about: The same chemistry in finer steps, each saying what the water is like: ideal 7.4-7.6, a task either side up to 7.2 and 7.8, a warning to 7.0 and 8.0, an error beyond, and critical (do not enter) below 5 or above 9.

bands.message: Highly acidic: corrosive to plaster, vinyl, metal fittings and skin; etches surfaces
Acidic: chlorine works well, but the water is uncomfortable and corrosive over time
Acceptable: the acidic side of ideal; chlorine very effective
Ideal: the best balance of comfort, chlorine and equipment life
Acceptable: the alkaline side of ideal; chlorine less efficient but still works
Mildly alkaline: chlorine much less effective; cloudy water and scale likely
Alkaline: chlorine mostly inactive, scale forms, eye and skin irritation common

profiles.name: Pool free chlorine (ppm)
profiles.about: Free chlorine in a swimming pool: 1-3 ppm is the usual target (the CDC's minimum is 1 ppm). Low lets germs through; high irritates eyes and skin, and above 10 ppm nobody should swim. ppm and mg/l are the same thing.

bands.message: Chlorine far too low: not safe to swim
Chlorine high: let it fall before adding more
Chlorine very high: wait before swimming
Chlorine far too high: don't swim

profiles.name: Hot tub free chlorine (ppm)
profiles.about: Free chlorine in a hot tub or spa: higher than a pool, as warm water breeds germs (Legionella among them). The CDC says 3-10 ppm; 3-5 is the usual target. Above 10 ppm, don't use it.

bands.message: Chlorine far too low: not safe to use
Chlorine high: let it fall before adding more
Chlorine far too high: don't use it

profiles.name: Hot tub bromine (ppm)
profiles.about: Bromine in a hot tub or spa, for those that use it instead of chlorine: the CDC says 4-8 ppm. Above 10 ppm, don't use it.

bands.message: Bromine far too low: not safe to use
Bromine high: let it fall before adding more
Bromine far too high: don't use it

profiles.name: Aquarium, tropical (°C)
profiles.about: A tropical freshwater tank: most community fish want 24-27 °C; a failed heater shows first as a slow fall.

bands.message: Tank far too cold: check the heater

profiles.name: Aquarium, cold water (°C)
profiles.about: A cold-water tank or pond (goldfish and the like): comfortable at 10-22 °C; warm water holds less oxygen.

profiles.name: Water softener salt (%)
profiles.about: A water softener's salt level, where it reports one as a percentage: top up below 25%; empty, it stops softening.

profiles.name: Indoor CO2 (ppm)
profiles.about: Carbon dioxide indoors, a measure of ventilation: under 1,000 ppm is good; over 1,500 ppm is stuffy and dulls thinking. Outdoor air is about 420 ppm, so a reading well under that means the sensor wants recalibrating.

bands.message: Reads below outdoor air: recalibrate the sensor

profiles.name: Indoor humidity (%)
profiles.about: Relative humidity indoors: 30-60% is comfortable; over 70% for long brings condensation and mould; under 30% dries skin and eyes.

profiles.name: PM2.5 (µg/m³)
profiles.about: Fine particles: the WHO's 24-hour guideline is 15 µg/m³; cooking, candles and wood burners push it up.

profiles.name: Radon (Bq/m³)
profiles.about: Radon gas: the UK's target level is 100 Bq/m³ and its action level 200 Bq/m³, above which the home should be fixed. A long-term average matters, hence the day's hold-off.

bands.message: Radon above the UK target level (100 Bq/m³)
Radon above the UK action level (200 Bq/m³): get it fixed

profiles.name: Freezer (°C)
profiles.about: A freezer should hold -18 °C or colder; a door opening or a defrost warms it briefly, hence the half-hour hold-off.

bands.message: Freezer too warm: check the door and seal

profiles.name: Fridge (°C)
profiles.about: A fridge should run at 0-5 °C; 8 °C is the UK legal limit for chilled food in shops and the line to keep under at home.

bands.message: Fridge far too warm: food at risk

profiles.name: Hot water cylinder (°C)
profiles.about: Stored hot water against Legionella: the HSE's guidance is to store it at 60 °C (Legionella grows at 20-45 °C); heat pumps often keep 50 °C with a weekly 60 °C cycle. Over 80 °C is a scalding risk.

bands.message: Hot water too cool: Legionella can grow
Hot water very hot: scalding risk

profiles.name: Boiler pressure (bar)
profiles.about: A sealed heating system's pressure: 1-1.5 bar cold, up to 2 bar hot. Low wants topping up (and a slow leak finding); near 3 bar the relief valve opens.

bands.message: Boiler pressure very low: top up, then find the leak
Boiler pressure very high: near the relief valve

profiles.name: Room temperature (°C)
profiles.about: Living space: 18-21 °C is comfortable; under 16 °C raises health risks (UK guidance), under 12 °C more so; over 28 °C is overheating.

profiles.name: Frost risk (°C)
profiles.about: An outdoor temperature: at 3 °C or below frost is likely (protect plants, cover the car); below -5 °C outside pipes and taps are at risk.

bands.message: Hard frost: protect outside pipes and taps

profiles.name: Unheated space, pipes (°C)
profiles.about: A loft, garage or outbuilding with water pipes: below 3 °C they're at risk of freezing and bursting.

profiles.name: Soil moisture (%)
profiles.about: A soil moisture probe's reading: rough, as probes and soils differ; adjust to your own. Most beds and lawns want 20-60%.

profiles.name: Wi-Fi signal (dBm)
profiles.about: A device's Wi-Fi signal strength: -67 dBm or better is solid; below -75 dBm drop-outs start; below -85 dBm it barely connects.

profiles.name: CPU temperature (°C)
profiles.about: A small computer's CPU (a Raspberry Pi throttles from 80 °C and hard at 85 °C): keep it under 70 °C with a case and airflow.

profiles.name: CPU use (%)
profiles.about: A computer's processor use (System Monitor's, or the Supervisor's for Home Assistant and each app): busy now and then is normal, so only a long stretch counts (a 15-minute hold-off).

profiles.name: Memory use (%)
profiles.about: A computer's memory use: past 90% for a while it starts swapping or killing things.

profiles.name: Disk used (%)
profiles.about: A disk's use: past 80% it's time to tidy; a full disk stops databases (Home Assistant's own among them).

profiles.name: Available (a task after an hour)
profiles.about: Only whether it's there, whatever its state: a bulb, a plug, anything with nothing else to go wrong. An hour's grace for one switched off at the wall.
profiles.message: Gone for an hour: is it switched off, or has it dropped off?

profiles.name: Available (critical)
profiles.about: Only whether it's there, for something that must be: a sensor an alarm or automation depends on. Also catches it being renamed or its integration removed.

profiles.name: Stays gone
profiles.about: The other way round: something retired or unplugged on purpose (an old relay, a device moved to another integration) that shouldn't come back.

available.message: It's back, and it should be gone

profiles.name: Security light on too long (on/off)
profiles.about: A security light that comes on with movement and goes off by itself: on for half an hour means it's stuck on (a sensor fault, a switch left on) or something keeps setting it off. Change the hold-off to suit its own timer.

on.message: Security light on for half an hour: stuck on, or someone about?

profiles.name: Reminder due (days)
profiles.about: A date something is due, read as the days until it: a spa's Rinse filter, Clean filter or Change water due (the Gecko integration's reminders), a service, a renewal. A task in the fortnight before, a warning in its week, an error once it's passed, critical a month after, until it's done and the date moves on. Watch the date entity (a timestamp sensor works too: tick A date: days until it in its editor).

bands.message: Overdue by more than a month

profiles.name: Electric car battery, 80% daily (%)
profiles.about: For most electric cars: Tesla (its Daily band; an LFP Tesla wants 100%, see LFP), Volkswagen, Skoda and Audi, Hyundai and Kia, BMW, Mercedes and GM's Equinox EV all advise charging to about 80% day to day and to 100% only before a long journey. Above 80% is a trip charge: a warning if it sits there. Under 20% a task (charge it tonight); under 10% an error.

bands.message: Battery very low: charge it now
Trip charge: over 80%, fine for a journey, not for sitting

profiles.name: Electric car battery, 90% daily (%)
profiles.about: For cars whose makers put the daily limit at 90%: Polestar (its car shows a charging tip once the limit is set at 90-100%) and Ford's Mustang Mach-E (its manual: 90% as the everyday charge); Rivian says 70-90%. Above 90% is a trip charge: a warning if it sits there. Under 20% a task; under 10% an error.

bands.message: Battery very low: charge it now
Trip charge: over 90%, fine for a journey, not for sitting

profiles.name: Electric car battery, LFP (%)
profiles.about: An LFP pack (lithium iron phosphate: a Standard Range Tesla, BYD's Blade battery, GM's new Bolt, many newer cars) is happy charged to 100%. Tesla's manual: keep the charge limit at 100%, even for daily use, and charge fully at least once a week, so the range estimate stays right (a Tesla's battery graphic shows 50% and 100% rather than Daily and Trip when it's LFP). Only low charge matters: under 20% a task, under 10% an error.

bands.message: Battery very low: charge it now
